prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the improper joinder doctrine requires the removing party to show there is no reasonable basis to predict recovery against the in-state defendant.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fifth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Defendants must show there is no reasonable basis to predict that Plaintiff might recover against the in-state defendant.**

A defendant may remove a case on diversity grounds only if no properly joined defendant is a citizen of the forum state. The improper joinder doctrine is a narrow exception to the rule of complete diversity. *Smallwood v. Ill. Cent. R.R. Co.*, 385 F.3d 568, 572–73 (5th Cir. 2004) (en banc). This Court has recognized two ways to establish improper joinder: "(1) actual fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts, or (2) inability of the plaintiff to establish a cause of action against the non-diverse party in state court." *Id.* at 573 (quoting *Travis v. Irby*, 326 F.3d 644, 646–47 (5th Cir. 2003)). Defendants allege no fraud in the pleading of jurisdictional facts, so only the second test applies. Under that test, the question is "whether the defendant has demonstrated that there is no possibility of recovery by the plaintiff against an in-state defendant, which stated differently means that there is no reasonable basis for the district court to predict that the plaintiff might be able to recover against an in-state defendant." *Id.*; accord *Campbell v. Stone Ins., Inc.*, 509 F.3d 665, 669 (5th Cir. 2007); *Cuevas v. BAC Home Loans Servicing, LP*, 648 F.3d 242, 249 (5th Cir. 2011).

**A. The burden rests on the removing party, and it is a heavy one.**

The removing party bears the burden. *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249; *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 574. That burden is "heavy." *Travis*, 326 F.3d at 649; *Campbell*, 509 F.3d at 669. It is heavy for good reason. Removal jurisdiction raises significant federalism concerns, so the removal statute is strictly construed. Any doubt is resolved in favor of remand. *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249; *Burden v. Gen. Dynamics Corp.*, 60 F.3d 213, 216–17 (5th Cir. 1995). The test asks about a reasonable possibility of recovery, not a mere theoretical one. *Campbell*, 509 F.3d at 669. Plaintiff is not required to show that she will win or is likely to win. She needs only a reasonable basis for predicting that state law might impose liability on the in-state defendant. *Id.*; *Griggs v. State Farm Lloyds*, 181 F.3d 694, 699–701 (5th Cir. 1999).

**B. The inquiry is a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis, and it does not become a merits trial.**

To decide whether the removing party has carried its burden, a court ordinarily "conduct[s] a Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis, looking initially at the allegations of the complaint to determine whether the complaint states a claim under state law against the in-state defendant." *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573; *see also Flagg v. Stryker Corp.*, 819 F.3d 132, 136–37 (5th Cir. 2016) (en banc) (confirming that the Rule 12(b)(6)-type analysis governs and applies the federal pleading standard to the improper joinder question). If the complaint survives that analysis, there is no improper joinder, and the inquiry ends. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 573. A court may "pierce the pleadings" only in a narrow set of cases. Even then, it may do so only to identify "discrete and undisputed facts that would preclude plaintiff's recovery against the in-state defendant." *Id.* at 573–74. The court must not use that limited inquiry to pretry the case. *Id.* at 574. The court also evaluates all factual allegations in the light most favorable to the plaintiff and resolves all contested issues of substantive fact and all ambiguities in state law in the plaintiff's favor. *Cuevas*, 648 F.3d at 249; *McDonal v. Abbott Labs.*, 408 F.3d 177, 183 (5th Cir. 2005); *Burden*, 60 F.3d at 216.

Defendants must also do more than point to a possible defense. A defense that may defeat the claim on the merits does not establish improper joinder unless it shows that the plaintiff has no reasonable possibility of recovery. *Larroquette v. Cardinal Health 200, Inc.*, 466 F.3d 373, 376 (5th Cir. 2006); *Davidson v. Ga.-Pac., L.L.C.*, 819 F.3d 758, 765 (5th Cir. 2016). The court should not resolve a defense that goes to the merits of the whole case when it would also dispose of the claims against the diverse defendants. *Smallwood*, 385 F.3d at 574. Doing so would decide the merits before the court has determined whether it has jurisdiction. *Id.*

**C. Application.**

Plaintiff's complaint alleges specific facts supporting each element of her state-law claim against the in-state defendant. Defendants have not identified any discrete and undisputed fact that would preclude recovery. They also have not shown that state law forecloses the claim. Under *Smallwood* and its progeny, that failure is dispositive. Defendants have not shown that there is no reasonable basis to predict that Plaintiff might recover against the in-state defendant. The in-state defendant was therefore properly joined, complete diversity is lacking, and the case must be remanded.
